pre.title: Before school: choose and register

note.title: Choose and register on time
note.text: Popular schools and concept schools (Montessori, Dalton, Jenaplan, Steiner, bilingual primaries) can have long local waiting lists, so check each school's registration rules early. Some schools keep their own early lists. Ask what such a list means at that school. In some cities there is a central procedure. In Amsterdam the municipality sends a letter and a form around the third birthday. You hand it in at your first-choice school by a deadline that depends on the birth date, and places follow priority rules and a lottery.

what: A child may start primary school at age 4. You can register from age 3, not earlier, and the Rijksoverheid asks you to register at least 10 weeks before the fourth birthday. You may register at more than one school. Some municipalities have their own registration rules and deadlines. Many schools let a child come for a few settling-in days from age 3 years 10 months, up to 5 in total, but not every school offers them. Compulsory attendance starts on the first day of the month after the fifth birthday.

Public schools are open to every child, if they have a place. Schools can have a waiting list or priority rules. A denominational or other "special" school works from a religion or belief. Both kinds can follow methods such as Montessori or Dalton.
todo: Visit two or three schools and read their school guide.
Ask each school how sign-up, priority rules and any waiting list work.

g12.title: Year groups 1 and 2
what: The first two years of primary school, which has eight year groups. Most children start on their fourth birthday.
todo: Nothing to sign up for.
Ask how the school decides when a child moves on to year group 3. The school decides, together with you.

g35.title: Year groups 3 to 5
what: The school keeps a record of your child's progress. The school advice in year group 8 is the school's judgement of that whole record.
todo: Ask for a talk once a year, and ask early if you are worried.
If the school suggests repeating a year, ask for the reasons in writing (see Questions).

g67.title: Year groups 6 and 7
what: Many schools start talking with parents about a likely secondary level around now. The formal advice is only given in year group 8.
todo: Ask the teacher when your school starts the conversation.
Look at secondary schools and their open days. Dates differ per school.

g8.title: Year group 8: advice, test and sign-up
what: In year group 8 the school gives a school advice (schooladvies) and your child takes an end-of-primary test. The advice can name one level or two, for example havo and vwo. You sign up at a secondary school with the final advice.
g8.whatDated: Dates for school year 2026-27. They are set again every year.
g8.afterSignup: Test results go to primary schools by 15 March 2027. After the sign-up week, placements start from 1 April 2027, and the secondary school decides on admission by 12 May 2027. In some regions registration can open earlier, but only with a final advice.

note.title: Act on time
note.text: Open days are usually in the winter, often January and February, and dates differ per school, so make a short list in the autumn. Cities such as Amsterdam, Utrecht and The Hague use central procedures with a lottery, so check your region's guide early and ask your child's school.

g8.whatUsual: The usual pattern: provisional advice in January, the test from late January into February, final advice in March, and sign-up at the end of March. The exact dates are set each year. For your child this is {label}.
todo: Visit open days and make a short list of schools that offer the advised level.
Ask how your region organises sign-up, and sign up within the sign-up week.

A secondary school may refuse a child only on limited grounds, such as having no places left. It may not use extra tests or IQ scores to refuse a child. Bilingual (tto) and top-sport schools may test for their specific skills.

vo1.title: First year of secondary school (brugklas)
what: Year 1 usually lasts one year, sometimes two. Many schools combine at least two levels in one class, for example vmbo-t with havo, or havo with vwo. Some schools are single-level and start in one level directly.
todo: Ask how and when a child can move up or down a level. The school decides.
Ask what extra support the school gives.

vo23.title: Years 2 and 3: choosing a pathway or profile
what: In vmbo, pupils choose a learning pathway (basis, kader, mixed or theoretical) and a sector by the end of year 2. In havo and vwo, pupils choose one of four profiles before the upper years: nature and technology, nature and health, economics and society, or culture and society. Schools usually ask at the end of year 3.
After year 3 of havo or vwo, a recognised pass certificate also gives access to mbo level 2, 3 or 4.
todo: Ask which profiles the school offers and which studies each one opens.
Moving between levels in these years is sometimes possible. The school decides.

fin.title: Exam year and what comes next
what: The final exam year is year 4 in vmbo (age 15 to 16), year 5 in havo (age 16 to 17) and year 6 in vwo (age 17 to 18). Practical education runs to about age 18.
todo: For mbo, apply to the programme by 1 April of the exam year. You can apply later, but then you have no right to admission.
For hbo or wo, check the subjects and application dates of each programme early.

he.title: After secondary school: mbo, hbo or wo
what: mbo (vocational college) has four levels: level 1 takes 1 year, level 2 takes 1 to 2, level 3 takes 2 to 3 and level 4 takes 3 to 4 years. A level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo.
hbo (university of applied sciences): a bachelor takes 4 years, and the first year is the first-year certificate (propedeuse). An associate degree takes 2 years. A master takes 1 to 2 years.

wo (research university): a bachelor takes 3 years and a master 1 to 3 years. A PhD usually takes about 4 years. A vwo diploma or a completed hbo first year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university. A havo diploma does not give direct entry. Some programmes also ask for particular subjects, and some select applicants. An hbo bachelor usually needs a bridging programme (pre-master) before a wo master.
Without the usual diploma, people from age 21 can usually ask for an admission test (21+ test). The institution decides and runs it.
todo: Check the entry rules, dates and any selection of each programme.

newc.when: First, usually for up to about two years
newc.unit: usually up to about two years

young.title: Newcomer class in primary school
young.what: Parents usually choose between a special language class (schakelklas) for children who just arrived, and a regular class with extra Dutch lessons. A temporary newcomer provision can enrol a child for at most 2 years in total.

old.title: Newcomer class in secondary school (ISK)
old.what: A special class at a regular secondary school for recently arrived pupils who speak little or no Dutch. Lessons are mainly Dutch, plus other subjects that prepare pupils for regular classes and for regular secondary or mbo education. Pupils usually stay up to about two years, then move to a regular class.

todo: Ask your municipality, a reception location or the nearest school where places exist.
Places can be limited in some cities, so ask early.

path.pro: Practical education (praktijkonderwijs): pupils can stay until the end of the school year in which they turn 18, and the Inspectie can allow an extension. Admission needs a declaration of eligibility (toelaatbaarheidsverklaring) from the regional partnership (samenwerkingsverband), not only the school advice. Next: the mbo entry programme (level 1, one year, no earlier diploma needed, for pupils who are 16 on 1 August) or a work route that the school arranges with the mbo college.
path.vbk: vmbo basis or kader: a diploma after 4 years. Basis leads to mbo level 2 (1 to 2 years). Kader leads to mbo level 3 (2 to 3 years) or level 4 (3 to 4 years), as the official entry requirements for 3 and 4 are the same. Programmes can add their own conditions, so ask the mbo college. A lower level is usually possible, and moving up later within mbo is possible.
path.vgt: vmbo gl/tl: a diploma after 4 years. Leads to mbo level 3 or 4. With one extra general exam subject, a diploma gives the right to enter havo. Without it, the havo school decides.
path.havo: havo: a diploma after 5 years. Leads to an hbo bachelor (4 years), an associate degree (2 years), mbo at any level, or vwo year 5 (a havo diploma gives the right to enter). A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo.
path.vwo: vwo: a diploma after 6 years. Leads to a wo bachelor (3 years), an hbo bachelor or an associate degree. Some studies ask for particular subjects or select applicants.

g8.more: Four dates this school year: 10 to 31 Jan, 25 Jan to 12 Feb, 24 Mar, 25 to 31 Mar 2027. Then placement from 1 April 2027 and the admission decision by 12 May 2027 (source: Rijksoverheid, VO-raad).
g8.text: Dates are set each year. Start visiting schools and ask your child's school for its calendar.

g67.text: Start looking at secondary schools now and ask the teacher when the conversation starts.

pre.title: Choose and register at a primary school
pre.text: You can register from age 3 and at least 10 weeks before the fourth birthday. Some municipalities, such as Amsterdam, have their own procedure and deadlines. Visit schools early and ask each how sign-up and any waiting list work.

early.title: First big step: school advice and secondary sign-up
early.text: Until then there is nothing to sign up for. Keep in touch with the teacher and ask early if you are worried about progress.

vo.title: No national deadline right now
vo.text: Level and profile choices are made by the school. Ask when they are made and what they mean for later studies.

fin.title: Apply to the mbo programme
fin.text: For mbo, apply by 1 April of the exam year to keep the right to admission. For hbo or wo, each programme sets its own dates.

he.title: Check dates and entry rules
he.text: Each programme sets its own application dates and entry rules.

dates.d: The school gives a provisional advice. Ask for a talk and ask what it is based on.

Your child takes the test at school. If the test advice is higher than the provisional advice, the school adjusts the advice upward, unless it explains why that is not in your child's interest. If the result is more than half a level higher, the school may choose a level in between.
The school sets the final advice. Secondary schools admit on this final advice.
Sign up at the secondary school you choose, with the final advice. Many regions allow more than one school, so check how yours works.

amsterdam.title: Amsterdam
amsterdam.text: Amsterdam runs a central lottery and matching procedure (centrale loting en matching) for secondary school. As we understand it, you rank schools that fit the school advice, each pupil gets a lot number, and places are matched using your ranking and the lot number. Do not assume the rules you know from another city apply here. The exact steps, the schools that take part and the dates change each year. Use the official Amsterdam sources and ask your child's school. Taking part is mandatory. How many schools you list depends on the advice. Pupils with a practical education advice do not take part in the lottery. Check the dates with OCO Amsterdam.

pupils.title: Pupils
pupils.expl: This is the number of children enrolled on the count date, 1 October. A bigger school is not better or worse than a smaller one. It does tell you how large the building and the year groups are likely to feel.
pupils.noCount: DUO did not publish a pupil count for this location.

advice.title: Where pupils go next: school advice
advice.expl: At the end of group 8, the school gives each child a school advice (schooladvies), the secondary level it recommends. The bar shows the advice given to the school's leavers. It describes the pupils the school has, not how good the school is. Schools with a different intake will show a different mix.

test.title: End-of-primary test (doorstroomtoets)
test.expl: In group 8 every child takes an end-of-primary test. Schools choose from several approved tests, and each test has its own scale. Never compare the score of one test with another. The average is context for the school advice, not a grade for the school.
test.note: Only compare schools that used the same test.
test.src: Source: DUO Open Onderwijsdata, test results

dist.title: How far pupils live
dist.expl: This is the straight-line distance between pupils' homes and the school. A small number means the school is mostly a neighbourhood school. A large number means pupils travel in from further away, which can matter for cycling and for friendships after school.
dist.median: Median distance from home to school
dist.src: Source: DUO Open Onderwijsdata, home-to-school distance

levels.title: Levels offered
levels.expl: Dutch secondary school has several levels. In vmbo there are four variants: basis and kader (more practical), and gl and tl (more theoretical). Then come havo (5 years) and vwo (6 years). A school can offer one level or several. A school with several levels under one roof makes it easier to move up or down later. The school decides on moving.
levels.none: The data does not list the levels of this location.
levels.atLeastNote: "At least" means DUO hides some small groups, so the real number is a little higher.
levels.fromPupilFile: Levels are taken from the pupil file.

pass.title: Exam results
pass.explShort: The national exam happens in the last year of each level. Pass rates depend on who the school admits and on how many candidates there are.
pass.expl: In the final year of each level, pupils sit the national exam. The pass rate is the share of candidates who passed. It also depends on which pupils the school admits and, for small groups, on chance. It is not a ranking, and a high rate is not the same as a good fit for your child.

insp.title: Inspection
insp.expl: The Dutch Inspectorate of Education visits schools and judges their quality. It mostly publishes a judgement after a visit, and visits are often triggered by concerns. So having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. Many schools are listed without a current final judgement, and that is not a rating. We do not rank, sort or average schools by it.

sbo.title: About special primary schools
sbo.text: A special primary school (sbo) is for children who need more support than a regular school can give. Admission needs a formal decision first. Ask your child's current school or your municipality.

so.title: Special education (SO and VSO)
so.expl: Special education has two parts. SO (speciaal onderwijs) is for children of primary-school age who need more support than a regular or special primary school (sbo) can give. VSO (voortgezet speciaal onderwijs) is the same for secondary-school age. Schools are grouped in four clusters by the kind of need they serve. A child can only be admitted with a formal decision called a toelaatbaarheidsverklaring (TLV), which the samenwerkingsverband (the regional partnership of schools that arranges extra support) issues. There are fewer of these schools than regular ones, so children often travel further.
so.noCount: Not shown (no count, or fewer than 5)
so.faqQ: How does my child get a place?
faqA: You cannot simply enrol your child. A toelaatbaarheidsverklaring (TLV) comes first. It is a formal statement that your child may attend special education.

The request is normally made together with the school your child attends now, with a description of your child's needs and of the support tried so far. The samenwerkingsverband of the region decides. If your child is not at a Dutch school yet, ask the school you have in mind, or the samenwerkingsverband of your area, where to start.

A TLV is valid for a set period and is reviewed, and some children later move back to regular education. Schools for clusters 1 and 2 work on a national basis, so the route can differ. Ask the school, and read the Rijksoverheid page on passend onderwijs.

lj.title: Pupils per year group
lj.note: Groups 1 and 2 are the youngest children (about 4 to 6 years). Group 8 is the last year before secondary school.

rn.title: Reading, language and maths levels
rn.expl: At the end of primary school the doorstroomtoets checks pupils against national reference levels. 1F is the fundamental level: the basics that every pupil should have by the end of primary school. 2F (reading and language) and 1S (maths) are the higher target level. National policy expects the basic level from every pupil and the higher level from a smaller group, the stronger pupils. So a school with fewer pupils at 2F or 1S than at 1F is normal, and the share at the higher level depends a lot on who the school admits.
rn.small: Small group: the percentages can swing a lot.
rn.note: Each bar is the share of tested pupils at that level or higher. A subject is left out when DUO hides a group of fewer than 5 pupils.
rn.src: Source: DUO, pupils per reference level for language and maths

hv.title: Advice reconsidered after the test
hv.expl: After the doorstroomtoets, a school must look again at its advice if the test result points to a higher level than the advice. This is called reconsideration (heroverweging). After the test the advice can only go up, never down. Reconsidering does not always change the advice.
hv.line: Advice reconsidered for {rec} leavers, raised for {rai}.
hv.of: Out of {n} group 8 leavers who took the test.
hv.noRatio: The two counts are shown separately and should not be turned into a percentage: DUO also counts some raised advices outside the group that was reconsidered.
hv.src: Source: DUO, reconsiderations and adjusted advice

ce.title: Central exam grades
ce.expl: The central exam (centraal examen, CE) is the national part of the final exam. This is the mean CE grade of the candidates, per level and exam year, on the Dutch scale of 1 to 10. Candidates need a CE average of at least 5.5, among other conditions, to pass. The mean also reflects which pupils the school admits.
ce.partial: Some small groups are left out.
ce.caption: Central exam grade {level}
ce.note: Each figure is approximate: it is the candidate-weighted average of the means DUO publishes per programme or profile. Groups with fewer than 5 candidates are left out.

zb.title: Repeaters and moves between levels
zb.expl: Some pupils repeat a year (zittenblijvers). Others move to a lower level (afstromers) or to a higher level (opstromers). Some movement is normal, especially in the first years, while the school confirms which level fits. The numbers do not say why pupils move, so use them as a question for the school.
zb.note: All levels together, for this location. DUO hides counts below 5.
zb.src: Source: DUO, repeaters and up- and down-streaming in secondary education

ov.title: Inspectie results (calculated)
ov.expl: Every year the Inspectie calculates three result measures for each type of secondary education at a location, from three years of data. They are compared with a norm that is corrected for the pupil population. This is not a judgement after a school visit, and not a ranking.

def.ob: The share of pupils who get through the first years (onderbouw) on time, without delay.
def.bb: The share of pupils who get through the upper years (bovenbouw) successfully, as the Inspectie calculates it from progress and exam data.
def.ce: The mean central-exam grade of the candidates, on the scale of 1 to 10.
def.verdict: A verdict the Inspectie derives from the three measures for this type of education: sufficient, insufficient, or insufficient unless a closer look shows otherwise. It is a calculation, not a judgement of the school.

ov.caption: Inspectie results {level}
ov.note: Norms are corrected for the pupil population, so they differ between schools. Being below a norm on one measure does not make a school weak. Ask the school about it. We do not rank or colour schools by these numbers.
ov.src: Source: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, onderwijsresultaten voortgezet onderwijs 2026 (CC0), three-year averages

op.title: Placement compared with the primary advice
op.expl: In year 3 the Inspectie compares the level each pupil is in with the level the primary school advised. The measure is the share of pupils placed above their advice minus the share placed below it, in percentage points. A negative number is common.
op.note: Compare the result with the norm only. A higher number means more pupils were placed above their advice relative to those placed below it.

sys.heading: The whole system on one page
sys.intro: Read from top to bottom. Each block is one school year. Every track has its own colour, and higher education has colours of its own, because finishing one school does not move a child on automatically: each change needs a diploma, an application and sometimes selection. No track is ranked above another.
sys.arrowNote: An arrow means a child can move that way. A solid arrow means the diploma normally gives the right to move. A dashed arrow means conditions, selection or a school decision apply. Letters and numbers match the list.
sys.title: The Dutch school system, top to bottom
sys.desc: Primary school of eight year groups leads, after school advice, to practical education, vmbo, havo or vwo. After those come mbo, hbo and wo. Arrows show how children can move between tracks.
sys.adviceLabel: School advice and sign-up, about age 12

xfers.text: After year group 8 (about age 12) the school advice and your sign-up decide the secondary track. The advice can name one level or two, such as havo and vwo.
Early years of secondary school: moving up or down a level is sometimes possible, and the school decides. Dashed because it is not a right.

vmbo gl/tl to havo: a gl or tl diploma with one extra general exam subject gives the right to enter havo. The extra subject cannot be a vocational subject or a school-specific programme. Without it, the havo school decides.

havo diploma to vwo: a havo diploma gives the right to join vwo year 5. A school may not set extra conditions for pupils who passed havo. Ask the vwo school about exemptions for subjects your child has already done.
Practical education to the mbo entry programme (level 1) or to work: the school arranges this with the mbo college.
vmbo diploma to mbo: basis leads to level 2. Kader, mixed or theoretical lead to level 3 or 4, because the official entry requirements for those are the same. A lower level is usually possible.
havo diploma to an hbo bachelor, an associate degree or mbo at any level. It does not give direct access to wo.
vwo diploma to a wo bachelor, or to an hbo bachelor or associate degree. Some studies ask for particular subjects or select.
An mbo level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo.
hbo first year (propedeuse) to a wo bachelor: a completed first year gives admission to a research university. Some programmes also ask for particular subjects, and some select applicants.
hbo bachelor to a wo master: usually through a bridging programme (pre-master). Length and cost differ per programme, and selection is possible.

sys.xfersExtra: Other arrows without a letter: bachelor to master and master to PhD. Selection is possible at each.

items.q: When must my child go to school?

blocks.p: A child may start at age 4. School is compulsory (leerplicht) from the first day of the month after the fifth birthday. It applies to every child who lives in the Netherlands, whatever the nationality.

Compulsory attendance ends at the end of the school year in which the child turns 16. After that, young people without a havo, vwo or mbo level 2 diploma must keep studying until they are 18 (kwalificatieplicht). If you live in the Netherlands but your child goes to a school abroad, for example in Belgium or Germany, you can ask your municipality's truancy officer for an exemption.
You then report every year that your child attends school abroad.

items.q: Which year group will my child join?

blocks.p: Not by a national rule. The old rule that a child joins group 3 depending on a 1 October birthday ended in 1985. Some schools still use a similar guide.

Today the school decides, together with you, and looks at age, development and earlier schooling. Children usually start in group 1 around the age of four and are in group 8 at about age 11. For a child who arrives from abroad, the school decides which year fits.
Ask how the school makes this decision, and what extra help your child gets for Dutch. The decision to move up or repeat a year is also the school's.

items.q: We arrive in the middle of the school year. Can my child still start?

blocks.p: Yes. Children can register at any time of the year. Secondary school registration also works at any time if you move house.

The school may have no places, so register at more than one school if you can. Special support or a place in a newcomer class can take time. For children who need extra support, register at least 10 weeks before the start date, in writing, and tell the school about the support right away.

The school then has 6 weeks to decide, and can extend this once by up to 4 weeks. Bring your child's passport, school reports and any proof of the previous school. If your child has no citizen service number (BSN) yet, the school can use a temporary education number.

items.q: Do I need a BSN or an address before I can register?

blocks.p: You register your child yourself and the school asks for your child's citizen service number (BSN). If your child has no BSN yet, the school can enrol your child with a temporary education number (onderwijsnummer), which DUO issues. Tell the school when your child gets a BSN.

If you live in the Netherlands, you get a BSN by registering with your municipality. Bring a passport, proof of address and de-registration or school reports from the previous school. In municipalities with a central procedure, such as Amsterdam, a proof of the future home address can be required.
Ask the school what it needs, and start early.

items.q: Can my child join a Dutch school without speaking Dutch?

blocks.p: Yes. What is on offer depends on age. In primary school, newcomers can join a language class or a transition class (taalklas or schakelklas), or a regular class with extra Dutch lessons.

In secondary school, pupils from age 12 who speak little or no Dutch can join an international transition class (ISK). Pupils learn Dutch and prepare for regular lessons. Many stay up to about two years, then move to a regular class.

Places can be limited in some cities, so ask early. Ask your municipality or a nearby school where places exist. Some schools also run special programmes for non-Dutch speakers, but bilingual schools can be hard for older children who start without Dutch.

items.q: Is repeating a year normal, and who decides?

blocks.p: The school decides whether a child moves up or repeats a year. There are no legal rules for it. The school guide describes how each school handles it. The school must tell you if your child repeats a year. If you disagree, you can object through the school's complaints procedure.

ul: Ask for the reasons in writing: which results and observations, and which support has been tried.
Ask for a meeting with the teacher and the school's learning-support coordinator (intern begeleider).
Repeating is not automatically good or bad. Ask the school what it expects to change.
If language is the issue, ask what support exists. Repeating a year may not fix a speech or pronunciation question, so ask the school and, if needed, a speech therapist.

blocks.p: We have no official figure for how common it is, so we do not give one.

items.q: Can I choose any primary school?

blocks.p: You can register at any school, and at more than one. There is no national catchment area. A school can be full, have a waiting list, or give priority to certain children.

Some municipalities have a central procedure. In Amsterdam, for example, priority goes first to a brother or sister already at the school, then to children from a linked playgroup, children of staff and children who live close by. A lottery decides when there are more applicants than places.
The school's admission policy is public, usually in the school guide or on its website. A public school is open to every child. Ask each school how it handles registration and waiting lists.

items.q: Can a religious school refuse my child?

blocks.p: A public school is open to every child, and its lessons are not based on a religion. A bijzondere (special) school teaches from a religion, a belief or a teaching concept, such as Montessori. The Rijksoverheid says a special school may require pupils and teachers to hold a religion or belief.
This applies only where it relates to the school's foundation. A school may not discriminate, for example on origin. A court decides in a dispute.
Read the school guide and ask about the admission policy before you register.

items.q: Can I choose any secondary school? Is there a catchment area?

blocks.p: You can register at any secondary school that offers the advised level. You may register at more than one, because a school can be full. A school may refuse a child only on limited grounds, such as having no places left.

It may not use extra tests or IQ scores. A bilingual (tto) or top-sport school may test only for its special skills. Some regions have agreements between schools on how pupils are spread, and places can be given by lottery.
Rules differ per region. Registration is usually in the sign-up week at the end of March. Ask your child's primary school how your region works.

items.q: Which cities use a lottery for secondary school?

blocks.p: Where a school has more applicants than places, a lottery can be used. Several large regions do, and the rules differ. Amsterdam places all pupils in one central round with a random lot number and a ranked list of schools.
Taking part is mandatory there. In the Utrecht regions a lottery is held at schools that have more first-choice applications than places. In 2026 this happened at twelve schools.
In Haaglanden eight schools drew lots in 2026. Rotterdam and Eindhoven have their own procedures. We could not confirm the rules for Haarlem or Nijmegen.
Procedures can change every year, so read the current guide of your region and ask your child's primary school.

items.q: How does the school advice work, and can I change it?

blocks.p: At the end of group 8 the school gives a school advice (schooladvies), based on your child's whole record. It can name one level or two, for example havo and vwo. In January the school gives a provisional advice.

Your child then takes the end-of-primary test. If the test advice is higher, the school adjusts the advice upward, unless it decides this is not in your child's interest, and then it must explain why. If the test result is more than half a level higher, the school may choose a level in between.
The school gives the final advice by 24 March 2027. A secondary school must place your child at least at the advised level, and may not require a one-level advice. The test cannot lower the advice.

items.q: How do I ask the school about the advice, or ask for a second opinion?

blocks.p: The school advice is the school's professional judgement of your child's whole record. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it does not raise it. Secondary schools admit on the final advice, and they may not ask a primary school to give an advice for one level only.

blocks.say: Could we meet to talk about the advice? Which results and observations is it based on? What would change it?

ul: Ask for the final advice and the reasons in writing.
Ask whether the learning-support coordinator can join the meeting.
Independent assessments exist, for example from a child psychologist or an assessment bureau. Costs and insurance cover vary a lot, so ask before you book.
The advice is only advice for the child's next school. Ask the secondary schools you like what they need to admit your child.

items.q: My child got a vmbo advice, what now?

blocks.p: vmbo takes 4 years and is a full route, not a dead end. After it comes mbo. The pathway matters: basis leads to mbo level 2, while kader, mixed or theoretical (gl/tl) lead to level 3 or 4. An mbo level 4 diploma gives the right to enter hbo, and a completed first hbo year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university, subject to programme requirements. That route takes more years than going straight through vwo, but every step exists.

ul: Ask which pathway the advice means: basis, kader or gl/tl.
Consider a school with several levels under one roof. A VO-raad factsheet argues that a broad first year keeps more options open. The school list shows this.
After vmbo gl/tl, a diploma with one extra general subject gives the right to join havo. Without it, the havo school decides.
The advice is the school's judgement. The end-of-primary test can raise it, and the school must explain if it keeps a lower one.

items.q: What is the difference between a Dutch school, an international school and a bilingual school?

blocks.p: A Dutch school teaches in Dutch and follows the Dutch curriculum. It is paid for by the state, and there are no tuition fees. An international school teaches in English or another language and often follows a programme such as the IB.

Dutch International Schools are partly government funded and meant for children of internationally mobile families. Fully private international schools set their own fees. A bilingual school (tto) is a Dutch secondary school where at least half of the lessons in the first years of havo and vwo are taught in English.

Pupils take the normal Dutch exams. Bilingual primary schools exist as a small pilot. Your choice depends on how long you will stay, your child's age and which language your child needs later. Nuffic's information on secondary bilingual education describes English. German and French are mentioned only for the primary pilot, and we could not confirm a Dutch-German secondary school.

items.q: What do international schools cost?

blocks.p: Dutch schools funded by the state do not charge tuition. International schools do. Private international schools set their own fees.

For 2026-27, one Amsterdam school (ISA) publishes tuition from about 22,800 euro a year in nursery to about 32,800 euro in the last two years. Some schools add other fees, such as a deposit. Dutch International Schools are partly government funded and usually cost less.

Third-party guides report about 4,500 to 9,500 euro a year, but we have not checked this against school fee schedules. Fees and admission rules differ per school and change every year. Ask each school for its current fee schedule and for the rules on who can apply.

items.q: I have the 30% ruling. Does that change school choice?

blocks.p: This site gives no tax advice. In general, employers can sometimes pay school fees for an international school tax-free as extraterritorial costs, under conditions set by the Belastingdienst. The conditions include the type of school and who it is meant for.

The 30% ruling is planned to become a 27% ruling from 2027, and the salary conditions change. Do not choose a school only because of a tax rule. Ask your employer's HR or a tax adviser before you sign a contract with a school, and read the current Belastingdienst pages.
State-funded Dutch schools charge no tuition, so there is nothing to reimburse for those.

items.q: Will my child's foreign school diplomas be recognised?

blocks.p: For study in the Netherlands, Nuffic compares a foreign diploma with a Dutch one. This is called a credential evaluation. It covers higher education and almost all secondary diplomas.

It is not binding. Dutch universities and universities of applied sciences decide who they admit, and they can add their own requirements, such as subjects or a language test. Ask the programme you want before you pay for an evaluation.
For school places, ask the school what documents it wants. Keep copies of reports and diplomas, with translations if needed.

items.q: Is Dutch school free? What is the ouderbijdrage?

blocks.p: State-funded schools do not charge tuition. Many ask for a voluntary parental contribution (ouderbijdrage) for extras such as trips, sports days or celebrations. It is voluntary.

Since a law of August 2021, a school may not exclude your child from activities because you did not pay, and may not offer a free replacement activity. The school guide should say this. You still pay for things that are not part of school, such as a private after-school club or lunch supervision.
Some families report pressure in practice. If that happens, point to the school guide and the Rijksoverheid information, and contact the parent council or the Rijksoverheid information line.

items.q: What are school hours and what happens at lunch?

blocks.p: Hours differ per school. Some primary schools have a continuous schedule (continurooster): all children stay at school during lunch, teachers supervise, and parents do not pay a lunch fee, although a voluntary contribution can be requested. Other schools have a break at midday.

Then children go home or stay for lunch supervision (overblijven or tussenschoolse opvang, TSO). The school must organise this on request, and parents pay a contribution. The parent council must agree with the amount.
Check the school guide for the weekly schedule, the lunch rules and the cost.

items.q: What about after-school care and childcare benefit?

blocks.p: After-school care (BSO) is separate from school. A BSO provider collects children from school and keeps them until parents finish work. You pay the provider.

The state can pay part of the cost through the childcare benefit (kinderopvangtoeslag), paid by the Belastingdienst. In 2026 the maximum hourly rate for BSO is 9.98 euro and the maximum benefit is 96 percent for lower incomes. The percentage falls as income rises.

The rules change from year to year, and conditions apply to your work, income and residence. Lunch supervision at school (TSO) does not count as childcare for the benefit. Check the current rules at the Belastingdienst before you sign a contract.

items.q: Can we take a holiday outside the school holidays?

blocks.p: Normally no, once your child is subject to compulsory education. The school head can give extra leave only if the nature of your work means you cannot take a family holiday in any school holiday, for example seasonal work. It is for up to 10 days, once per school year.
Apply at least 8 weeks before the trip. Leave is not possible in the first two weeks of the school year. If you take your child out without permission, you can be fined.

The Rijksoverheid does not give an amount, so ask your municipality's truancy officer. A child of 4 is not yet subject to compulsory attendance, but ask the school what it expects. Longer absences are not allowed under this rule.

items.q: My child needs extra support. What are my rights?

blocks.p: Dutch schools have a duty of care (zorgplicht). The school where you register your child must offer a suitable place, in the school itself or at another school. Schools work together in regional partnerships (samenwerkingsverbanden passend onderwijs).

Register in writing at least 10 weeks before the new school year and tell the school about the support your child needs. The school has 6 weeks to decide and can extend this once by up to 4 weeks. If you disagree with the plan, you can involve your regional partnership.
Special primary schools (sbo) and special schools need a formal declaration of eligibility (toelaatbaarheidsverklaring) first. A practical education (praktijkonderwijs) advice needs one too.

items.q: What does "university" mean here (wo vs hbo)?

blocks.p: Dutch higher education has two kinds. wo is the research university: more theory, and a bachelor takes 3 years. hbo is the university of applied sciences: more practice, and a bachelor takes 4 years. Outside the Netherlands both are often called "university", so check which one a document means.

ul: vwo is the usual route to wo. havo leads to hbo. An mbo level 4 diploma also gives the right to enter hbo.

A havo diploma alone does not give access to wo. A vwo diploma or a completed hbo first year (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university. Some programmes also ask for particular subjects, and some select applicants.
Without the usual diploma, people from age 21 can usually ask for an admission test (the 21+ test). The institution decides and runs it.

items.q: Can my child study in English at university?

blocks.p: Yes, many programmes at Dutch universities and universities of applied sciences are taught in English. Study in NL keeps a database of English-taught programmes. Entry still depends on your diploma.

A vwo diploma or a completed first year of hbo (propedeuse) gives admission to a research university, and a havo or mbo level 4 diploma gives access to hbo. Some programmes ask for particular subjects, a language test or selection. For a foreign secondary diploma, check the requirements of the programme, and ask for a Nuffic credential evaluation if the institution wants one.

groups.title: Reading the numbers on this site

items.q: How should I read the numbers on this site?

blocks.p: The numbers are context for a talk with the school, not a ranking. Pupil counts, school advice, exam results and distances come from DUO open data. To protect privacy, DUO hides groups of fewer than 5 pupils, so a blank or "fewer than 5" means the group is hidden.
Small groups also make percentages swing a lot. A school advice mix describes the pupils a school has. It does not say how good the school is.

Exam pass rates depend on who the school admits. Inspection judgements come from the Inspectie van het Onderwijs. A school without a judgement has simply not been rated yet, and that is not a bad sign.
The site never sorts schools by best.

sources.heading: Data and sources
sources.intro: Where the numbers and rules on this site come from, how to read them, and what we are not.

check.title: Check with the school and your municipality
check.text: Last checked: {date}. This page was written with AI assistance. Facts checked against official sources (Rijksoverheid, DUO, Inspectie, VO-raad, Nuffic and others) on 10 November 2026. Where sources differ, the page says "usually" or "most schools". Rules and dates change every year; check with the school and your municipality.

read.title: How to read the numbers
items: DUO, the Dutch education agency, hides any count below 5 pupils to protect privacy. When you see "fewer than 5", "at least" or "partial", some small groups are missing, so the real figure is a little higher.

The numbers are context for a conversation with a school, not a ranking. A high exam pass rate or a particular school advice mix also reflects which pupils the school admits. We never sort or colour schools by quality.

An Inspectie judgement is only published after a school visit, and visits are often triggered by concerns. Having a judgement, or not having one, says little by itself. Where a school has several programme judgements, we show the lowest one as a summary. That is our own rule, not an Inspectie rule, and the judgement for each programme is shown next to it.

Many schools are listed by the Inspectie without a current final judgement (Geen eindoordeel) or under basic supervision (Basistoezicht). That is not a rating and not a bad sign. We say so in words and never show it as a score.

blocks.title: What each part of a profile comes from
blocks.intro: Each block on a school profile comes from one open dataset. The periods are those of the files we used.
items: Pupils per year group and the pupil trend: DUO, pupils per location and year group, 2021-2022 to 2025-2026 (count date 1 October).

Special education (SO and VSO): DUO address file and pupils per cluster and age, 2025-2026. The type, the cluster and the pupil counts come from DUO. Support profiles and admission criteria are not open data per school and are not shown.
Reading, language and maths levels: DUO, pupils per reference level for language and maths, 2025-2026. Advice reconsidered: DUO, reconsiderations and adjusted advice, 2025-2026.
Central exam grades: DUO, exam results 2021 to 2025. Repeaters and level moves: DUO, 2024-2025 to 2025-2026.

Inspectie results and placement against the primary advice: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, onderwijsresultaten voortgezet onderwijs 2026 (CC0). Three-year averages, with the Inspectie's norms and calculated verdicts.

Inspection judgements and standards: Inspectie van het Onderwijs, open data oordelen, 1 November 2026 (CC0). The English names of the standards are our own short glosses of the Inspectie's Dutch names.

none.title: No current final judgement

basic.title: Basic supervision (no separate final judgement)
basic.expl: The school is under basic supervision. In the Inspectie's data this is a school that earlier had the judgement Goed, which has expired. It has no separate final judgement now. This is not a rating.
